concept.name: Onion Architecture

relationships.description: Connects Onion Architecture to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: An architectural style that places domain entities and business rules at the center, forcing all dependencies—frameworks, databases, and UI—to point strictly inward through interfaces.
spark.keyTakeaway: Isolate your core business logic from Spring, SQLAlchemy, or Kafka by defining repository and gateway interfaces inside the domain/application ring and implementing them in the outermost infrastructure ring.

concept.whyItMatters: In traditional N-tier architectures, business services directly import ORM entities and database clients, coupling domain rules to schema quirks and framework lifecycles. When you upgrade Hibernate, swap PostgreSQL for DynamoDB, or test complex pricing rules, you end up booting a 6-second application context or mocking SQL cursors. Onion Architecture inverts those dependencies so pure domain logic compiles and runs in under 15 milliseconds with zero I/O.
whenToUse: Core business domains with rich invariants, state machines, or regulatory rules (e.g., billing ledgers, underwriting, order fulfillment) that outlive web frameworks.
Long-lived services where swapping persistence engines, message brokers, or external vendor APIs (e.g., Stripe to Adyen) must not require rewriting business logic.
Teams that want fast, deterministic unit tests for 80%+ of their codebase without spinning up Docker/Testcontainers for every rule variation.
whenNotToUse: Simple CRUD microservices, admin backends, or BFFs where 90% of the code is validating JSON and writing rows to a single table.
Short-lived prototypes, hackathons, or early-stage MVPs where mapping between domain objects, DTOs, and ORM models slows down iteration.
Read-heavy reporting or analytics pipelines (e.g., dbt, Spark jobs) whose primary job is executing set-based SQL transformations rather than enforcing entity invariants.
keyPoints: The Dependency Rule is absolute: source code dependencies may only point inward toward the Domain Model; inner rings never import classes from outer rings.
The Domain Model ring holds pure entities, value objects, and domain events with zero framework annotations (no `@Entity`, `@Column`, or `@Autowired`).
The Domain Services and Application Services rings orchestrate use cases and define output ports (interfaces like `PaymentGateway` or `OrderRepository`).
The Infrastructure and UI rings sit on the outside, implementing those ports with concrete adapters (JPA, jOOQ, gRPC, Kafka consumers, FastAPI routers).
Boundary enforcement should be automated in CI using tools like ArchUnit (Java) or import-linter (Python) so accidental outer-ring imports fail the build.

examples.title: Payment Ledger Migration from MySQL/JPA to CockroachDB
examples.scenario: A fintech ledger service originally coupled Hibernate `@Entity` classes directly to settlement rules. Moving to multi-region CockroachDB required changing transaction retry semantics and primary key generation.
examples.outcome: After refactoring to Onion Architecture, settlement invariants lived in pure Java `LedgerEntry` aggregates while `JpaLedgerRepository` implemented a `LedgerRepository` port. Swapping in a jOOQ-based CockroachDB adapter took 4 days with zero changes to the 340 domain unit tests.

examples.title: ArchUnit Guardrails in a Spring Boot Order Service
examples.scenario: As an e-commerce team grew from 6 to 30 engineers, developers began injecting `RestTemplate` and `KafkaTemplate` directly into domain calculators, causing 9-second test boots and circular dependencies.
examples.outcome: Adding an ArchUnit `onionArchitecture()` check in Gradle CI rejected 14 PRs that leaked `org.springframework` or `jakarta.persistence` into `..domain..`, cutting the core test suite runtime from 42 seconds to 1.8 seconds.

tradeOffs.pro: Domain logic stays completely portable and free of ORM lazy-loading surprises or framework magic.
tradeOffs.con: Requires explicit mappers between domain aggregates, persistence entities, and API DTOs—adding 15–25% more files per feature.

tradeOffs.pro: In-memory fakes implementing repository ports run thousands of business-rule tests in milliseconds.
tradeOffs.con: Mocks and fakes can drift from real SQL constraints (unique indexes, lock behavior), so contract tests against real DBs are still mandatory.

tradeOffs.pro: Write-side aggregates enforce strict transactional consistency without leaking SQL into domain rules.
tradeOffs.con: Complex paginated reads or joins feel awkward through pure repository ports and often need a dedicated CQRS read-model bypass.

failureModes.name: Anemic Domain Model
failureModes.description: Engineers strip behavior out of domain entities into giant Application Services, leaving entities as dumb getter/setter bags while duplicating validation across use cases.
failureModes.mitigation: Push invariant checks and state transitions (`order.confirm()`, `wallet.debit(amount)`) directly onto domain aggregates and keep Application Services thin.

failureModes.name: Leaky ORM Abstractions
failureModes.description: Putting `@Entity` or `@JsonProperty` annotations on domain classes or returning Hibernate `PersistentBag` proxies from repositories ties domain behavior to an active DB session.
failureModes.mitigation: Maintain separate persistence models in the infrastructure package and map explicitly at the repository boundary.

failureModes.name: Mapping Fatigue & N+1 Regressions
failureModes.description: Blindly loading full aggregate graphs through generic `findById()` ports for simple read endpoints causes severe N+1 query storms.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Onion Architecture for command/write paths and allow slim, read-only query projections (CQRS) that map SQL rows straight to response DTOs.

failureModes.name: Architectural Drift in Growing Teams
failureModes.description: Without automated checks, urgent hotfixes introduce direct imports from `infrastructure` into `domain`, silently collapsing the onion back into a big ball of mud.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce ring boundaries in CI with ArchUnit (`Architectures.onionArchitecture()`) or Python `import-linter` contracts.

commonMistakes: Confusing runtime call flow with compile-time dependency direction—outer controllers call inner services, but inner services depend only on interfaces.
Creating a 1:1 `IRepository` interface for every database table instead of designing ports around aggregate roots.
Putting transaction boundaries (`@Transactional`) inside domain entities instead of wrapping use cases in the Application Service or an outer decorator.
Over-abstracting standard library utilities (e.g., wrapping `java.time.Clock` is useful for tests, wrapping `StringUtils` is pure noise).
Using MapStruct or reflection mappers blindly across boundaries, hiding missing fields until runtime.

sections.content:
## The idea

Coined by Jeffrey Palermo in 2008, **Onion Architecture** solves a recurring rot in layered N-tier systems: the database sits at the bottom of the dependency graph, so every layer above it—business logic, services, and UI—transitively couples to SQL schemas and ORM frameworks.

Onion Architecture flips the graph using the **Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)**. Instead of the domain depending on a `PostgresOrderRepository`, the inner rings define an `OrderRepository` interface (port), and the outer infrastructure ring provides `PostgresOrderRepository` (adapter). Everything compiles from the outside in, while the core remains pure language primitives and domain types.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an e-commerce `PlaceOrder` use case handling inventory reservation and payment capture:

1. **UI / Web Ring (`OrderController`)**: Deserializes the HTTP `POST /orders` payload into a `PlaceOrderCommand` and invokes `PlaceOrderUseCase.execute(cmd)`.
2. **Application Service Ring (`PlaceOrderUseCase`)**: Starts a transaction boundary, loads the `Cart` via the `CartRepository` interface, and calls `Order.createFrom(cart)`.
3. **Domain Model Ring (`Order`, `Money`)**: Pure Java/Python objects verify that `cart.items()` is non-empty, compute totals using `Money` value objects, and transition status to `PENDING_PAYMENT`.
4. **Infrastructure Ring (`JpaOrderRepository`, `StripePaymentAdapter`)**: Implements the interfaces defined inside the application/domain rings, translating `Order` into a `orders` table row and calling Stripe's `/v1/payment_intents` API.

data.title: Inward Dependency Direction vs. Runtime Execution Flow

edges.label: 1. Dispatch Command
edges.title: Controller invokes Use Case
edges.description: Maps JSON request to a framework-free PlaceOrderCommand and calls the application service.

edges.label: 2. Enforce Invariants
edges.title: Execute pure domain logic
edges.description: Domain aggregate validates line items, discounts, and state transitions with zero I/O.

edges.label: 3. Call Port Interface
edges.title: Polymorphic dispatch to adapter
edges.description: Application service calls OrderRepository.save(), which routes at runtime to the Postgres adapter.

edges.label: 4. Implements Port (DIP)
edges.title: Compile-time inward dependency
edges.description: Infrastructure imports the Application/Domain port interface; the domain never imports SQL or Stripe.

edges.label: 5. Return Result DTO
edges.title: Return outcome to caller
edges.description: Returns OrderId and status without leaking JPA entities or internal exceptions to the HTTP layer.

data.caption: Runtime control flows from UI through Application Services to Infrastructure adapters, while compile-time source dependencies point strictly inward toward the Domain Model.

sections.content:
## Anatomy of the four rings

Each ring has a strict boundary on what it may import:

- **Domain Model (Center)**: Entities, Value Objects, Aggregates, and Domain Events. Allowed imports: language standard library only.
- **Domain Services**: Stateless business logic spanning multiple aggregates (e.g., currency conversion policies or FX spread calculations).
- **Application Services**: Use-case orchestrators (`PlaceOrderUseCase`), transaction coordination, and output port interfaces (`OrderRepository`, `EventPublisher`).
- **Infrastructure & UI (Outer)**: Web controllers, CLI handlers, JPA/SQLAlchemy repositories, Kafka producers, and DI wiring (`Spring @Configuration` or FastAPI `Depends`).

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Onion vs. Layered vs. Hexagonal vs. Clean
sections.content:
## Onion vs. Layered vs. Hexagonal vs. Clean

| Dimension | Classic N-Tier | Onion Architecture | Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) | Clean Architecture |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Dependency Direction** | Top-down (UI -> Biz -> DB) | Strictly inward toward Domain | Symmetric inward toward Core | Strictly inward toward Entities |
| **Core Organizing Unit** | Database tables & services | Domain Model & Services | Application Core + Ports | Entities & Use Case Interactors |
| **Framework Coupling** | High (ORM leaks into services) | Zero in inner 3 rings | Zero inside hexagon | Zero inside Entities/Use Cases |
| **Primary Strength** | Fast initial CRUD scaffolding | Rich domain modeling (DDD) | Clean I/O & protocol swapping | Explicit use-case boundaries |
| **CI Enforcement Tooling** | Rarely enforced | ArchUnit `onionArchitecture()` | ArchUnit / import-linter | ArchUnit / module boundaries |

## Failure modes

1. **Bypassing Reads Through Heavy Aggregates**: Fetching a 12-table aggregate just to render a 3-column summary table kills DB performance. Keep Onion ports for write commands and allow a direct read-only query service for dashboards.
2. **Framework Annotations Creeping Inward**: Adding `@Transactional`, `@Validated`, or `@Entity` into the domain package defeats portability and reintroduces 5-second test boots.
3. **Leaky Exceptions**: Letting `PSQLException` or `DataIntegrityViolationException` bubble uncaught through a repository port forces the Application Service to import database driver packages to handle unique-key conflicts; translate them into domain exceptions like `DuplicateOrderException` inside the adapter.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Enforcing boundaries with ArchUnit and Python Protocols
sections.content:
## Enforcing boundaries with ArchUnit and Python Protocols

Conventions decay unless CI rejects violations. In Java/Kotlin, **ArchUnit** provides a first-class rule:

```java
Architectures.onionArchitecture()
  .domainModels("com.acme.orders.domain.model..")
  .domainServices("com.acme.orders.domain.service..")
  .applicationServices("com.acme.orders.application..")
  .adapter("persistence", "com.acme.orders.infra.postgres..")
  .adapter("rest", "com.acme.orders.infra.web..");
```

In Python, define ports as `typing.Protocol` classes inside `domain/ports.py` and enforce unidirectional package imports in CI using `import-linter` (`type = layers`), ensuring `domain` never imports `sqlalchemy`, `fastapi`, or `boto3`.

## Practical checklist

- **Zero framework imports in `domain/`**: Verify with `grep` or ArchUnit that no ORM, HTTP, or DI annotations exist inside the domain package.
- **Separate persistence models**: Map between `Order` (domain) and `OrderJpaEntity` (infrastructure) at the repository boundary.
- **Translate infrastructure errors**: Convert SQL unique-constraint or HTTP 429 errors into domain-meaningful exceptions inside adapters.
- **Use CQRS for heavy reads**: Let read-only reporting endpoints bypass aggregate hydration via slim query projections.
- **Automate in CI**: Fail pull requests automatically on any outward dependency violation.

interviewProblems.title: Onion Architecture
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Onion Architecture. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: An architectural style that places domain entities and business rules at the center, forcing all dependencies—frameworks, databases, and UI—to point strictly inward through interfaces.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Domain Model Core applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Postgres & Stripe Adapters.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Postgres & Stripe Adapters experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Push invariant checks and state transitions (`order.confirm()`, `wallet.debit(amount)`) directly onto domain aggregates and keep Application Services thin.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Isolate your core business logic from Spring, SQLAlchemy, or Kafka by defining repository and gateway interfaces inside the domain/application ring and implementing them in the outermost infrastructure ring.
Avoid trap: Confusing runtime call flow with compile-time dependency direction—outer controllers call inner services, but inner services depend only on interfaces.
Avoid trap: Creating a 1:1 `IRepository` interface for every database table instead of designing ports around aggregate roots.
When to reach for it: Core business domains with rich invariants, state machines, or regulatory rules (e.g., billing ledgers, underwriting, order fulfillment) that outlive web frameworks.
When to reach for it: Long-lived services where swapping persistence engines, message brokers, or external vendor APIs (e.g., Stripe to Adyen) must not require rewriting business logic.

putItTogether.title: Putting Onion Architecture Together
putItTogether.summary: Isolate your core business logic from Spring, SQLAlchemy, or Kafka by defining repository and gateway interfaces inside the domain/application ring and implementing them in the outermost infrastructure ring.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Onion Architecture before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: After refactoring to Onion Architecture, settlement invariants lived in pure Java `LedgerEntry` aggregates while `JpaLedgerRepository` implemented a `LedgerRepository` port. Swapping in a jOOQ-based CockroachDB adapter took 4 days with zero changes to the 340 domain unit tests.
